rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A Lewis structure is an electron audit made visible. Count the valence electrons (adjusting for charge), pick the least electronegative central atom, spend electrons on bonds first and outer octets second, park the remainder on the centre, and promote lone pairs to double or triple bonds when the central octet falls short.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Total valence e⁻ = Σ(valence e⁻) ± charge - FC = V − (N + ½B) - Domains = bonding pairs + lone pairs (central atom)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Draw lone pairs first, shapes later:** every VSEPR answer begins with the completed Lewis structure — lone pairs included — or the domain count collapses.  ·  **Formal charge vs oxidation state:** FC assigns bonding electrons equally; oxidation state assigns them to the more electronegative atom — the two bookkeeping systems give different numbers on purpose.

rows.text: Electron budget quickies: H₂O/NH₃/CH₄ = 8; CO₂ = 16; BF₃ = 24; PCl₅ = 40; SF₆ = 48. "Least EN central, H always terminal."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2022 & 2024 (2m): Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. What is its molecular shape?** — Carbon dioxide has 4 + 2(6) = **16 valence electrons**. Skeleton O–C–O: one pair in each C–O link, six electrons (three lone pairs) on each oxygen complete their octets but leave carbon with only four.…  ·  **NEB 2024 (3m): Draw the Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ and predict their shapes using VSEPR theory.** — **H₂O:** 8 valence electrons → two O–H bonding pairs plus **two lone pairs** on oxygen.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: In shape questions, write three lines: Lewis structure → electron domains (bonds + lone pairs) → shape + angle with the lone-pair compression remark. That structure matches the mark scheme.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The Lewis structure is the input to VSEPR: bonding pairs + lone pairs = electron domains. Lone pairs on the central atom are the difference between electron geometry and molecular shape — omit them and every downstream answer is wrong.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Procedure: count valence e⁻ (± charge) → skeleton (least EN central) → bonds → outer octets → leftovers on central atom → double/triple bonds if short → verify. Gallery: H₂O (2 LP, bent), NH₃ (1 LP, pyramidal), CH₄ (tetrahedral), CO₂ (2 C=O, linear), BF₃ (6 e⁻, trigonal planar), PCl₅ (10 e⁻, TBP), SF₆ (12 e⁻,…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: BF₃'s 6-electron boron is the textbook Lewis acid: it completes its octet by accepting NH₃'s lone pair, forming the NH₃·BF₃ adduct.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Compute the formal charges in the ozone molecule and state what they imply.** — For O₃ (central O double-bonded to one O, single-bonded to the other): central O = 6 − (2 + 3) = **+1**; double-bond terminal O = 6 − (4 + 2) = **0**; single-bond terminal O = 6 − (6 + 1) = **−1**.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Chemistry in Dots and Lines A Lewis dot structure is a molecule's electron budget made visible: every valence electron accounted for, either as a bonding pair (a line) or a lone pair (dots). Draw it correctly and the shape, polarity and reactivity of the molecule follow almost mechanically.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The drawing procedure 1. **Count** total valence electrons (adjust for charge: add for anions, subtract for cations). 2. **Choose the skeleton** — least electronegative atom central (H is always terminal). 3. **Place one bond pair** between every connected pair; complete the octets (duets for H) of outer atoms with lone pairs. 4.…  ·  ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote | |---|---|---| | **Lewis structure** | Diagram of valence electrons as dots/lines showing bonding and lone pairs | CO₂: O=C=O | | **Lone pair** | Valence pair not shared between atoms | H₂O: 2 LP | | **Bonding pair** | Electron pair shared between two atoms | CH₄: 4 BP | | **Formal charge** | FC =…

rows.text: "A Lewis structure represents valence electrons as dots, with shared pairs drawn as lines, such that each atom attains its octet (or a recognised exception)."  ·  Draw the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion and identify the formal charges.  ·  Why must hydrogen always occupy a terminal position in a Lewis structure?

rows.text: Draw SO₂ and explain why sulphur carries a lone pair despite two S=O-style links.  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Verified PYQ (NEB 2022 & 2024): Lewis dot structure of CO₂ and its shape - Count: 4 + 2(6) = **16 electrons**. - Skeleton O–C–O; place one pair in each C–O bond (4 e⁻), complete O octets with lone pairs (12 e⁻) — carbon has only 4 e⁻.…  ·  ## 5. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Lone pairs are not optional decoration:** omitting them changes the VSEPR count and hence the predicted shape — H₂O without its lone pairs would be drawn "linear" and lose all the marks.  ·  **Total electrons ≠ electrons shown as dots around one atom:** in CO₂ the 16 electrons distribute over three atoms; the audit line "used = counted" is the safety check.  ·  **Formal charge ≠ real charge:** it is a bookkeeping index for choosing among structures; the molecule's real charge distribution comes from electronegativity (partial charges), not FC.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 7. Exam Application **Verified PYQ (NEB 2022/2024): Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. What is its molecular shape?** — 16 valence electrons; O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen; carbon's octet completed by two double bonds.…  ·  **Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Draw the Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ and predict their shapes using VSEPR theory.** — H₂O: two bonds + two lone pairs → bent, ≈104.5°. NH₃: three bonds + one lone pair → pyramidal, ≈107°.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Draw the Lewis structure of BF₃ and comment on boron's octet.** — 24 valence electrons; three B–F single bonds, three lone pairs on each F; boron holds only 6 electrons — an incomplete octet, making BF₃ a strong Lewis acid that completes its octet by accepting a pair (e.g. from NH₃).
